title: The Repaired Palate and the Public Sphere: Gummersbach, Frankfurt, Starnberg
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rhineland Boyhood and the Westwall

stops.name: Düsseldorf, the birth and the cleft palate
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia give the birth at Düsseldorf on 18 June 1929, with a cleft palate corrected by surgery in childhood. No hospital or street is documented in any source consulted; the coordinate is the city.
stops.campa: A son is born at Düsseldorf on the eighteenth of June, in the Rhine Province of a republic with four years left to run. The child has a cleft palate. Surgeons close it in his childhood, and the operations leave him with a speech that strangers have to work to follow. No hospital and no street are recorded anywhere consulted. What is recorded is the palate, the surgery, and the difficulty afterward, and that seventy-five years later, in Kyoto, he will trace his account of language back to it: not to a theory, but to the experience of depending on other people to finish his sentences.
suggested_refs: The Kyoto Prize commemorative lecture of 11 November 2004, in which Habermas himself traced two motifs of his thought to the childhood operation
sources: kyotoprize.org, laureate page for Jürgen Habermas

stops.name: Gummersbach, the Deutsches Jungvolk
stops.date_confidence: attested for the membership: de.wikipedia has him in the Deutsches Jungvolk from the age of ten, which gives 1939; month and day are unrecorded and defaulted to 01 January. One strand of the research pool compressed two separate dates into this one, since de.wikipedia dates the appointment as Jungvolkführer only from 1943 and specifies the role as first-aid instructor. The father's NSDAP membership from 1933 is de.wikipedia and was omitted from that strand.
stops.campa: The family lives at Gummersbach, east of Cologne, Protestant and provincial, where his father Ernst directs the chamber of commerce and has held a party card since 1933. Nobody in the house is a fanatic and nobody resists. At ten the boy enters the Deutsches Jungvolk along with every other boy of his year, a child with a repaired palate inside a movement that prizes physical soundness. By 1943 he wears the braid of a Jungvolkführer, and the work they give him is first aid: bandaging, splints, the treatment of burns.
suggested_refs: Ernst Habermas (1891-1972), director of the Gummersbach chamber of commerce, NSDAP member from 1933

stops.name: The Westwall, the anti-aircraft detachment
stops.date_confidence: text attested, place reconstructed. en.wikipedia, verbatim: 'From August 1944, his detachment operated anti-aircraft guns against the Allied advances on the Siegfried Line.' No source consulted names a site, a battery or a village. The research pool carried two different invented coordinates for this single event, 49.6/6.9 in the Trier and Konz sector on the Luxembourg border and 50.7/6.3 in the Aachen and Düren sector; the second is used because it lies within reach of Gummersbach and of the autumn 1944 advance, and it is a regional placeholder rather than a landmark. Day within August unknown, defaulted. The February 1945 evasion of Wehrmacht conscription is de.wikipedia and has no place recorded at all.
stops.campa: In August the fifteen-year-old goes west with his detachment to serve anti-aircraft guns against the armies coming up out of France. No source consulted names the village or the battery. He is a schoolboy in uniform feeding shells to a gun, and the line he is defending is a row of concrete teeth laid across farmland; the detachment is made up of boys from his own school year, under men too old for the front. In February 1945 the Wehrmacht calls him up. He does not go, and hides until the Americans arrive.
suggested_refs: The Westwall fortifications of the Aachen and Düren sector, defended by Flakhelfer detachments of schoolboys in the autumn of 1944

stops.name: Gummersbach, the Abitur at the Gymnasium Moltkestraße
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia gives the Abitur at Easter 1949 at the Gymnasium Moltkestraße in Gummersbach. Easter Sunday 1949 fell on 17 April; 1 April is used as an ordering date inside the Easter term, not as a documented day. An earlier reading of the pool guessed the town's Lindengymnasium from the Wikipedia article on Gummersbach; that guess is wrong and is not followed here.
stops.campa: Four years separate the flak battery from the leaving certificate. The Nuremberg trials run through his sixteenth and seventeenth years; the camp films are shown in every occupied zone, and the archives of the state he drilled for are opened and read aloud on the radio. He is nineteen when he takes his Abitur at the Gymnasium Moltkestraße at Easter, in a country whose rubble is still being cleared by hand. Easter Sunday falls that year on the seventeenth of April, and the day of the examination itself is not recorded. In the autumn he enrolls at Göttingen.
suggested_refs: The Gymnasium Moltkestraße, Gummersbach, named by de.wikipedia as the school of the 1949 Abitur

stops.name: Göttingen, the first matriculation
stops.date_confidence: attested that he studied philosophy, history, psychology, German literature and economics at Göttingen from 1949 (en. and de.wikipedia). No month or day is recorded; the autumn term of 1949 is an ordering date. The coordinate is the Alte Aula on Wilhelmsplatz, the university's ceremonial building, standing in for an enrollment whose faculty address is not documented; the pool's alternative city-centre point, 51.5328/9.9352, lies about a kilometre south and is used in this file only for the 2023 stop.
stops.campa: He matriculates at Göttingen in philosophy, history, psychology, German literature and economics, the full spread of a Bildung degree taken by a student who does not yet know which of the five he will keep. The university survived the war nearly intact and is filling with veterans and with boys too young to have been veterans. Its faculty was denazified on paper and staffed, in large part, by the same men. What he read in these two years, and with whom, is nowhere recorded. He stays until 1950 and then leaves for Zürich.
suggested_refs: The Alte Aula of the University of Göttingen, Wilhelmsplatz

stops.name: Zürich, the year across the border
stops.date_confidence: attested that he continued his studies at the University of Zürich (en.wikipedia), dated 1950 in the research pool. No month or day is recorded and the autumn term is an ordering date. Coordinate is the university's main building at Rämistrasse 71.
stops.campa: For a year he studies at Zürich, in the university's main building on the Rämistrasse above the old town, out of Germany for the first time and in a city that spent the war as a neutral reading room and kept its emigres and their libraries. The Swiss university was never denazified because it never needed to be. Göttingen had been, on paper. He is twenty-one, still working inside the German idealist line, and what he is working toward is Schelling. Then he crosses back over the border to Bonn.
suggested_refs: The main building of the University of Zürich, Rämistrasse 71

stops.name: Bonn, the last years of study
stops.date_confidence: attested that he completed his studies at Bonn under teachers including Erich Rothacker and Oskar Becker (en. and de.wikipedia), and that he met Ute Wesselhoeft there as a fellow student. Month and day unrecorded; the autumn term of 1951 is an ordering date. Coordinate is the Kurfürstliches Schloss, the university's main building. Karl Löwith's part in turning him from the Heideggerian idiom toward the young Marx is carried by the research pool without a page reference and is not a documented teaching relation; Löwith held his chair at Heidelberg, not Bonn.
stops.campa: The last stretch of his studies runs at Bonn, in the elector's palace on the Rhine, in the provisional capital of a state four years old. His teachers are Erich Rothacker, who had signed for the regime and gone on lecturing afterward, and Oskar Becker, a mathematician turned phenomenologist out of Husserl's Freiburg. What no teacher there does for him, the writing of Karl Löwith does: it turns him out of the Heideggerian idiom and toward the young Marx. In the same corridors he meets a fellow student, Ute Wesselhoeft.
suggested_refs: Karl Löwith, Von Hegel zu Nietzsche (1941), the book that carried the young Marx back into postwar German philosophy

stops.name: Bonn, the article against Heidegger in the FAZ
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and venue: de.wikipedia records that Habermas published in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung in 1953, reviewing the newly republished Einführung in die Metaphysik and objecting that Heidegger had left the phrase on the 'inner truth and greatness' of the movement unrevised. The month and day are not in the research pool and are defaulted to 01 January. One strand of the pool gave the place simply as 'Germany' with Bonn coordinates and dropped the newspaper, which is the load-bearing detail. The stop sits at Bonn because that is where Habermas was; the paper is Frankfurt's and no travel was required.
stops.campa: Heidegger reprints his 1935 lecture course without touching the sentence about the inner truth and greatness of the National Socialist movement, and adds not a word about the eighteen years in between. A doctoral student of twenty-four writes to the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung and asks in public how the most important philosopher in Germany can set that line in type again in 1953 and say nothing. It is the first thing he publishes that gets read outside Bonn. Heidegger does not answer him, then or afterward.
suggested_refs: Heidegger's 1935 Freiburg lecture course Einführung in die Metaphysik, republished unaltered in 1953
The unrevised phrase on the 'innere Wahrheit und Größe' of the movement, pinned at Freiburg in Heidegger's own record

stops.name: Bonn, the Schelling dissertation
stops.date_confidence: attested: doctorate in philosophy at Bonn in February 1954 with the dissertation Das Absolute und die Geschichte. Von der Zwiespältigkeit in Schellings Denken (en.wikipedia, Britannica). The day within February is not recorded and is defaulted. The marriage to Ute Wesselhoeft is dated 1955 by de.wikipedia and is reported inside this stop rather than given one of its own, since no place beyond Bonn is recorded for it.
stops.campa: The thesis is on Schelling: the absolute and history, and the split running through Schelling's thinking between a God who is finished and a world that is still happening. It is written wholly inside the German idealist tradition by a man who has just accused that tradition's living heir, in a national newspaper, of bad faith. The following year he marries Ute Wesselhoeft, whom he met here as a student. Then he takes work as a freelance journalist and does that for the next two years.
suggested_refs: Das Absolute und die Geschichte. Von der Zwiespältigkeit in Schellings Denken (Bonn dissertation, 1954)

stops.name: Frankfurt, Senckenberganlage, assistant to Adorno
stops.date_confidence: attested: research assistant to Theodor Adorno at the Institute for Social Research from February 1956 (en.wikipedia, Britannica); the day within the month is not recorded and is defaulted. The coordinate is the Institute building on the Senckenberganlage and is inherited unchanged from the pins already fixed at this address for Adorno and for Horkheimer. de.wikipedia gives the assistantship as 1956 to 1961, not to 1959 as one strand of the research pool had it; he leaves for Marburg and Heidelberg in 1961.
stops.campa: He arrives at the Institute for Social Research as Theodor Adorno's assistant, into a building put up again on the Senckenberganlage by men who had come back from California. Adorno he takes to at once, and the debt runs both ways for the rest of Adorno's life. Max Horkheimer, who directs the house, reads the new assistant's politics and does not care for what he reads. The money that built the place had come from Buenos Aires, out of the grain fortune of Felix Weil's father.
suggested_refs: The rebuilt Institut für Sozialforschung, Senckenberganlage 26, Frankfurt am Main

stops.name: Frankfurt, the three children
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the three births: Tilmann in 1956, Rebekka on 3 July 1959 at Frankfurt am Main, Judith in 1967 (de.wikipedia, 'Jürgen Habermas', with the exact day from de.wikipedia, 'Rebekka Habermas'). The stop is dated to 1956 and carries all three, since only Rebekka's day is recorded; month and day for 1956 are unknown and defaulted. One strand of the research pool gave the place for Rebekka and Judith as 'Germany' while already carrying Frankfurt coordinates; Frankfurt is used for all three, the household being there in those years.
stops.campa: Three children are born to Jürgen and Ute Habermas across eleven years: Tilmann, who becomes a psychologist and a professor of psychoanalysis; Rebekka, born on the third of July 1959, who becomes a historian of the nineteenth century and of German colonialism; Judith, who becomes a designer. Their father is at this point an assistant on a temporary contract whose superior is working to end his academic career. The household moves when the contract moves, from Frankfurt to Marburg to Heidelberg and back to Frankfurt inside four years.
suggested_refs: Rebekka Habermas (1959-2023), professor of modern history at Göttingen

stops.name: Frankfurt, Student und Politik and the blocked habilitation
stops.date_confidence: attested that the empirical study Student und Politik, on the political consciousness of Frankfurt students, was published in 1961 (Britannica), and that Horkheimer resisted both its appearance under the Institute's name with Habermas's introduction and the habilitation at Frankfurt (en.wikipedia, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). Month and day not recorded, defaulted. The Institute's own memorial notice of 2026 states that eight habilitation attempts failed before Marburg accepted the thesis; that figure appears in no other source consulted and is reported as the Institute's count.
stops.campa: The survey asks Frankfurt students what they take politics to be, and finds a democracy inhabited by people nobody has asked to want one. At issue between the two men is whether critical theory may still say in public what it thinks of the society that pays for it. Horkheimer will not let the study out under the Institute's name with Habermas's introduction attached, and will not have him habilitate in his house. Sixty-five years later the Institute's own death notice counts eight failed habilitation attempts before a place is found for him.
suggested_refs: Student und Politik (1961), the Institute study whose introduction Horkheimer refused to publish under the Institute's imprint

stops.name: Marburg, Abendroth takes the habilitation
stops.date_confidence: attested that Habermas habilitated at Marburg under the sponsorship of Wolfgang Abendroth in 1961, the thesis published in 1962 as Strukturwandel der Öffentlichkeit (SEP, en. and de.wikipedia). Month and day not recorded, defaulted. Three coordinates for the university circulate in the research pool, 50.8021/8.7666, 50.8021/8.7719 and 50.8108/8.7736, spanning some 800 m; the first is used and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Wolfgang Abendroth, the one declared Marxist holding a chair in the Federal Republic, accepts the thesis Frankfurt would not accept. What it treats had not previously been treated as an object at all: the public sphere, the coffee houses and newspapers and reading societies in which private people constituted themselves as a public and argued their way to a claim on the state. The book traces that formation, and then traces its refeudalization by press concentration and public relations. It appears in 1962 under the title Strukturwandel der Öffentlichkeit.
stops.quote: The bourgeois public sphere may be conceived above all as the sphere of private people come together as a public.
stops.quote_source: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere: An Inquiry into a Category of Bourgeois Society, trans. Thomas Burger with Frederick Lawrence (MIT Press, 1989), p. 27.
suggested_refs: Strukturwandel der Öffentlichkeit (1962), the Marburg habilitation thesis

stops.name: Heidelberg, the chair and the quarrel with Gadamer
stops.date_confidence: attested: an extraordinary professorship in philosophy at Heidelberg, secured with the help of Hans-Georg Gadamer and Karl Löwith, held until the 1964 move to Frankfurt (en.wikipedia, Britannica). The research pool gives the start as both 1961 and 1961/62; the month is not recorded and the autumn term of 1961 is used as an ordering date. The debate with Gadamer over ideology critique and the limits of hermeneutic tradition is attested in the pool's geographic strand without dates for its individual exchanges.
stops.campa: Gadamer and Löwith get him the Heidelberg chair, and Gadamer gets an opponent for his trouble. Wahrheit und Methode has just appeared, arguing that understanding always takes place inside a tradition the understander cannot step outside of. Habermas answers that a tradition can also be a system of distortion, and that a critique of ideology needs exactly the standpoint hermeneutics refuses to grant. Neither man converts the other. The exchange runs in print for a decade.
suggested_refs: Hans-Georg Gadamer, Wahrheit und Methode (1960), and the Habermas-Gadamer debate on hermeneutics and ideology critique

segments.name: Horkheimer's Chair and the Student Years

stops.name: Frankfurt, Bockenheim, Horkheimer's chair
stops.date_confidence: attested: returns to Frankfurt in 1964 as successor to Max Horkheimer's chair in philosophy and sociology (en.wikipedia, Britannica); month and day not recorded, defaulted. The coordinate is Campus Bockenheim at 50.1191/8.6520, from de.wikipedia's article on the campus. The research pool's 50.1197/8.6633 is roughly 800 m east, near the Taunusanlage, and is not used anywhere in this file; the pool's own correcting note establishes the point.
stops.campa: Three years after Horkheimer refused him a habilitation, Habermas is appointed to Horkheimer's chair in philosophy and sociology. He is thirty-five, and he comes to it from an extraordinary professorship at Heidelberg that lasted three years. The Bockenheim campus he teaches on is filling with the first cohort large enough to be called a student movement, and his lecture halls are the fullest in the faculty. Adorno is still directing the Institute across the Senckenberganlage, a five-minute walk away.
stops.quote: a realm of private individuals assembled into a public body
stops.quote_source: 'The Public Sphere: An Encyclopedia Article' (1964), trans. Sara Lennox and Frank Lennox, New German Critique, No. 3 (Autumn 1974), p. 53.
suggested_refs: Campus Bockenheim, Goethe University Frankfurt, seat of the philosophy faculty until the 2001 move to Westend

stops.name: Frankfurt, the inaugural lecture on knowledge and interest
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the Frankfurt inaugural lecture Erkenntnis und Interesse was delivered on 28 June 1965, and the book of the same title followed in 1968 (Britannica, cross-checked against the Wikipedia publication chronology). The book is reported inside this stop rather than given one of its own, since the research pool records no place for its publication beyond Frankfurt. The quote is verified at plato.stanford.edu, cited there as (1968b: 9 [1971a: vii]).
stops.campa: The inaugural lecture argues that knowledge is never disinterested, and that the interests are not corruptions of it. A technical interest in controlling nature produces the empirical sciences. A practical interest in reaching understanding produces the historical and hermeneutic ones. An emancipatory interest in freedom from constraint produces critique. Positivism, by this argument, is not a mistake about method but a refusal to ask what the method is for. Three years later the argument fills a book of the same title.
stops.quote: That we disavow reflection is positivism.
stops.quote_source: Knowledge and Human Interests, trans. Jeremy J. Shapiro (Beacon Press, 1971), preface, p. vii.
suggested_refs: Erkenntnis und Interesse, inaugural lecture of 28 June 1965 and book of 1968

stops.name: Hanover, the congress and the phrase
stops.date_confidence: attested: the congress 'Bedingungen und Organisation des Widerstands' met at Hanover on 9 June 1967, a week after Benno Ohnesorg was shot in West Berlin on 2 June, and there Habermas clashed with Rudi Dutschke, warning of a 'verhängnisvolle Strategie' and a 'Scheinrevolution' (de.wikipedia). The German phrase he used is 'linker Faschismus', not the 'Linksfaschismus' one strand of the pool printed, and de.wikipedia records that he later withdrew it; dropping that retraction would leave the entry one-sided. No venue within Hanover is named in the sources; the coordinate is the city centre.
stops.campa: A policeman has shot a student in the back of the head in West Berlin, and the movement gathers at Hanover a week later to decide what resistance now means. Rudi Dutschke argues for direct action, for a voluntarism that manufactures its own conditions. Habermas answers that this is a doomed strategy and a sham revolution, and, in the room, calls it left fascism. He spends the following years having the phrase quoted back at him by students he agrees with about nearly everything else. He takes it back.
suggested_refs: The Hanover congress 'Bedingungen und Organisation des Widerstands', 9 June 1967

stops.name: Frankfurt, the directorship refused
stops.date_confidence: attested that Adorno died in August 1969, that Habermas declined the directorship of the Institute for Social Research, and that he proposed Leszek Kołakowski for the post without success (en. and de.wikipedia). The month is set to August, after the death, as an ordering device; no day is recorded for the refusal. The stop is placed at the university and not at Adorno's grave in the Frankfurter Hauptfriedhof, since Habermas's presence at that burial is not attested in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Adorno dies in Switzerland at the end of a year in which his own students occupied his institute and he called the police to clear it. The directorship falls to Habermas by every expectation in Frankfurt, and he refuses it. No source consulted records a reason he gave in public. He puts forward Leszek Kołakowski, the Polish philosopher expelled from Warsaw the year before, and Frankfurt will not have him. The directorship goes to others, and Habermas keeps the chair he already holds.
suggested_refs: Adorno's grave in the Frankfurter Hauptfriedhof, 7 August 1969
Leszek Kołakowski, expelled from the University of Warsaw in 1968

stops.name: Frankfurt, the letter to Marcuse
stops.date_confidence: attested in the geographic strand of the research pool, from en.wikipedia: in 1971 Habermas wrote to Herbert Marcuse marking a break with the inherited Frankfurt School formation while remaining within critical theory's problem field. No month or day is given and none is inferred; 01 January 1971 is an ordering date. Adorno had written his own letter to Marcuse on 5 May 1969, two years earlier and out of the same institutional crisis; the two are distinct documents to the same recipient and are not to be conflated.
stops.campa: He writes to Herbert Marcuse in California to say what he is doing, which is leaving. Not leaving critical theory: leaving the family arrangement, the school with founders and heirs and a canon of its own. What survives the break is the question the Institute was built to ask, why an enlightened society keeps reproducing domination. What goes is the answer inherited from Weber and Lukács. Marcuse is being read by students on two continents that year, and Habermas had argued against him at Hanover four years earlier. He writes back.
suggested_refs: Adorno's letter to Marcuse of 5 May 1969, a distinct document to the same recipient two years earlier

segments.name: Starnberg: the Institute for Living Conditions

stops.name: Starnberg, the Max Planck Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested: scientific member and, with Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, director of the Max-Planck-Institut zur Erforschung der Lebensbedingungen der wissenschaftlich-technischen Welt at Starnberg from 1971 (SEP, mpg.de). The English name has to carry 'living conditions'; the research pool's shorter rendering drops the phrase that explains what the place was for. Month and day not recorded, defaulted. The coordinate is the town; the institute building's address was not confirmed in any source consulted. Marcuse's own record places yearly meetings with Habermas here from 1974 at 47.9997/11.3438, some 250 m away.
stops.campa: The Max Planck Society builds him an institute on a lake south of Munich and sets it to study the living conditions of the scientific and technical world. He directs it with Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, a physicist who had worked on the German uranium project and spent the rest of his life on what that meant. There is no teaching and there are no students. There are research groups, a budget, and ten years. The two volumes of the Theory of Communicative Action are written here. Herbert Marcuse comes out from California every year from 1974.
stops.quote: The task of universal pragmatics is to identify and reconstruct universal conditions of possible mutual understanding.
stops.quote_source: On the Pragmatics of Communication, ed. Maeve Cooke (MIT Press, 1998), p. 21.
suggested_refs: The Max-Planck-Institut zur Erforschung der Lebensbedingungen der wissenschaftlich-technischen Welt, Starnberg, 1971-1981

stops.name: Starnberg, Legitimationsprobleme im Spätkapitalismus
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1973 (Britannica); month and day not recorded, defaulted. The place is the Starnberg institute where Habermas was then working, not a documented place of composition, and the research pool gives no place for the publication at all.
stops.campa: The book asks what a state does once it has taken responsibility for an economy it cannot control. It can shift the crisis out of the economic system and into the political one, where it shows up as a shortage of something that cannot be printed: reasons why anyone should obey. Late capitalism, on this account, runs a deficit in legitimacy the way an earlier capitalism ran one in capital. The German title says late capitalism; the English edition drops the qualifier and calls the book Legitimation Crisis.
suggested_refs: Legitimationsprobleme im Spätkapitalismus (1973), translated as Legitimation Crisis

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Hegel Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested that Habermas received the Hegel Prize in 1973 (de.wikipedia). The prize is awarded by the city of Stuttgart, Hegel's birthplace, and the coordinate is the city; no ceremony venue and no date within the year appear in any source consulted, so month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: The prize is the city of Stuttgart's, given in the town where Hegel was born, and it goes to a philosopher who has spent twenty years arguing with Hegel's inheritance without once stepping outside it. What he keeps from Hegel is the claim that reason is something a society does, in institutions and over time, and not something a mind possesses. What he refuses is the ending: the arrival, the reconciliation that closes the account and lets the philosopher stop. He is forty-four.
suggested_refs: The Hegel Prize of the city of Stuttgart

stops.name: Frankfurt, Paulskirche, the Adorno Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested. de.wikipedia, 'Theodor-W.-Adorno-Preis': the prize of the city of Frankfurt is conferred on 11 September in the Paulskirche, and Habermas is the 1980 laureate, delivering 'Die Moderne, ein unvollendetes Projekt'. An earlier reading of the research pool treated the Paulskirche as merely the customary venue and tagged the stop a reconstruction; the venue is constituted by the prize, so the tag is upgraded to attested. The coordinate lies within about 130 m of the church. Adorno's own record notes Habermas as the 1980 winner by name.
stops.campa: Frankfurt gives the prize named for Theodor Adorno to the assistant Adorno took on in 1956. He speaks in the Paulskirche, where the first German national assembly sat in 1848 and got nowhere, and he answers everyone then declaring the Enlightenment finished. Modernity, he says, is not a failed period but an unfinished project; its promises were not refuted by the twentieth century, they were abandoned by intellectuals who found the abandonment more interesting. The lecture is called 'Die Moderne, ein unvollendetes Projekt'.
suggested_refs: 'Die Moderne, ein unvollendetes Projekt', the Adorno Prize lecture of 11 September 1980, Paulskirche, Frankfurt

stops.name: Starnberg, Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1981, in two volumes (en.wikipedia, Britannica); month and day not recorded, defaulted. Written during the Starnberg directorship, which the same sources place from 1971 to 1981, and the coordinate is the institute town rather than a documented place of composition. The quote is verified at plato.stanford.edu, cited there as (1981 [1984a: 280]); the research pool's page range 'c. 280-287' is imprecise and is pinned here to p. 280.
stops.campa: Two volumes, eleven hundred pages, published in 1981. Reason is not a possession of the individual mind. It is what happens between people who are trying to reach an understanding, and who can only do that by raising claims the other is free to refuse. The pathologies of modern life, on this reading, are not an excess of reason but reason confined to one of its uses. On that footing he builds the second half of the argument: a lifeworld of shared meanings, and systems of money and administrative power that grow into it and take it over.
stops.quote: Reaching understanding is the inherent telos of human speech.
stops.quote_source: The Theory of Communicative Action, Vol. 1: Reason and the Rationalization of Society, trans. Thomas McCarthy (Beacon Press, 1984), p. 280.
suggested_refs: Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns, 2 vols. (1981)

stops.name: Starnberg, the resignation and the closed institute
stops.date_confidence: attested: Habermas resigned the Starnberg directorship in April 1981, after von Weizsäcker's retirement and amid institutional conflict, and the Max Planck Society closed the institute in May 1981 (mpg.de, cross-checked against en.wikipedia and Britannica). The day within April is not recorded and is defaulted. The research pool's range '1971-1981/82' is corrected here to 1971-1981.
stops.campa: Von Weizsäcker retires. The arrangement that made the place work was the two of them together, and the Society and the remaining director do not agree about what the institute is now for. Habermas resigns in April; in May the Society closes the institute altogether. Ten years of funded research into the living conditions of the scientific and technical world end in a dispute over governance. The two volumes came out a few months earlier. He is fifty-one, and he holds no post.
suggested_refs: The closure of the Starnberg Max Planck Institute, May 1981

stops.name: Berkeley, the California interval
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The research pool records a period at the University of California, Berkeley between the Starnberg resignation and the 1983 return to Frankfurt, sourced only to en.wikipedia and given without dates. No month, day, department or appointment type was found in any source consulted, and 1982 is an ordering date between two attested events rather than an attested one.
stops.campa: Between the closed institute and the Frankfurt chair there is a stretch in California, at Berkeley, where American philosophy has been reading him for a decade and arguing back in a vocabulary he is learning to answer in. The pragmatist line, Peirce and Mead and Dewey, is already inside The Theory of Communicative Action; here it is spoken in the corridor rather than footnoted. How long he stayed, on what terms, and what he taught are not recorded in anything reachable.
stops.quote: Science can only be comprehended epistemologically, which means as one category of possible knowledge.
stops.quote_source: Knowledge and Human Interests, trans. Jeremy J. Shapiro (Beacon Press, 1971), p. 4.
suggested_refs: The pragmatist inheritance in The Theory of Communicative Action: Peirce, Mead, Dewey

segments.name: The Return to Frankfurt and the Public Quarrels

stops.name: Frankfurt, Bockenheim, the chair again
stops.date_confidence: attested: a chair at Goethe University Frankfurt from 1983 until the 1994 retirement (en. and de.wikipedia, Britannica); month and day not recorded, defaulted. Moralbewusstsein und kommunikatives Handeln appears in 1983 and Der philosophische Diskurs der Moderne in 1985; the second is reported inside this stop, the research pool giving it no place beyond Frankfurt. Coordinate is Campus Bockenheim per de.wikipedia; the pool's 50.1197/8.6633 is not used. Foucault died on 25 June 1984, before the lectures were published.
stops.campa: He comes back to the same faculty and teaches in it for eleven years. Discourse ethics is worked out in these years with Karl-Otto Apel: a moral norm is valid only if everyone affected could accept it in a discussion nobody is coerced in. In 1985 he publishes twelve lectures on the philosophical discourse of modernity, opening with Hegel, the first to make modernity a philosophical problem, and closing with the French thinkers he takes to have given the problem up. Michel Foucault has been dead a year and cannot answer him.
stops.quote: We understand a speech-act when we know what makes it acceptable.
stops.quote_source: The Theory of Communicative Action, Vol. 1, trans. Thomas McCarthy (Beacon Press, 1984), p. 297.
suggested_refs: Der philosophische Diskurs der Moderne (1985), twelve lectures from Hegel to the French present
Moralbewusstsein und kommunikatives Handeln (1983), the discourse ethics worked out with Karl-Otto Apel

stops.name: Hamburg, Die Zeit and the Historikerstreit
stops.date_confidence: the article is attested to the day; the place is a reconstruction and very probably not a place he was. de.wikipedia, 'Historikerstreit': 'Eine Art Schadensabwicklung: Die apologetischen Tendenzen in der deutschen Zeitgeschichtsschreibung' appeared in Die Zeit on 11 July 1986, attacking Ernst Nolte, Andreas Hillgruber, Michael Stürmer and Klaus Hildebrand. Submitting an article required no travel; the coordinate is the newspaper's home city, not a documented visit. One strand of the research pool dropped Hildebrand from the four; he is restored.
stops.campa: Four historians have been arguing, in respectable venues, that the extermination of the European Jews was a reaction to a Bolshevik precedent, that German suffering in the east deserves a commemoration of its own, and that a nation needs a usable past. Habermas answers on 11 July in a Hamburg weekly and calls it a settling of accounts, a damage claim filed on behalf of national feeling. He is not a historian and does not pretend to be one; what is in dispute is what a republic may tell itself. The quarrel runs for two years through every serious German newspaper.
suggested_refs: 'Eine Art Schadensabwicklung', Die Zeit, 11 July 1986, the opening of the Historikerstreit

stops.name: Frankfurt, Faktizität und Geltung
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1992 (en.wikipedia, Britannica); month and day not recorded, defaulted. The place is the Frankfurt chair, not a documented place of composition. The 1995 exchange with John Rawls, 'Reconciliation through the Public Use of Reason', is carried in the research pool as a reconstruction with no place attached at all, and is reported inside this stop rather than pinned anywhere.
stops.campa: Thirty years after the book on the public sphere he writes the book on what a legal order would have to be for that sphere to matter. Law is where the discourse principle becomes an institution: legitimate law is law that could be agreed to by the people it binds, through procedures they can actually enter. Private autonomy and public autonomy are not rivals to be balanced against each other, since neither exists without the other. Three years later he and John Rawls, who had reached neighbouring conclusions from the other end of the century, conduct an exchange about it in print.
stops.quote: I would in fact tend to have more confidence in the outcome of a democratic decision if there was a minority that voted against it, than if it was unanimous... Social psychology has amply shown the strength of this bandwagon effect.
stops.quote_source: 'Further Reflections on the Public Sphere,' in Craig Calhoun (ed.), Habermas and the Public Sphere (MIT Press, 1992), p. 441.
suggested_refs: Faktizität und Geltung (1992), translated as Between Facts and Norms
The 1995 Habermas-Rawls exchange, 'Reconciliation through the Public Use of Reason'

stops.name: Berlin, the march against the asylum law
stops.date_confidence: attested: Habermas joined a Berlin demonstration of roughly 350,000 people against the restriction of asylum rights on 8 November 1992 (de.wikipedia). No assembly point is named in any source consulted; the coordinate is the Brandenburg Gate, the standard rallying point for demonstrations of that scale in the period, and it stands in as a placeholder rather than as a confirmed route.
stops.campa: Two years after unification, with hostels burning at Hoyerswerda and Rostock and the Bundestag preparing to write the right of asylum out of the constitution, three hundred and fifty thousand people fill central Berlin. Through the Historikerstreit he had argued that the only patriotism left available to Germans was attachment to a constitution rather than to a people, and the article now being amended is in that constitution. The philosopher of the public sphere is one of the marchers, sixty-three years old, on foot in the crowd on the eighth of November.
stops.quote: In political usage, the concepts 'nation' and 'people' have the same extension. But in addition to its legal definition, the term 'nation' has the connotation of a political community shaped by common descent, or at least by a common language, culture, and history. A people becomes a 'nation' in this historical sense only in the concrete form of a particular form of life.
stops.quote_source: The Inclusion of the Other: Studies in Political Theory, ed. Ciaran Cronin and Pablo De Greiff (MIT Press, 1998).
suggested_refs: The Asylkompromiss of 1992-93 and the amendment of Article 16 of the Basic Law

stops.name: Frankfurt, the emeritus
stops.date_confidence: attested: retirement from the Frankfurt chair in 1994 (en.wikipedia, Britannica); month and day not recorded, defaulted. The first tranche of the Vorlass, covering the work up to this retirement, reached the university library in 2011, per Goethe University's own announcement.
stops.campa: He retires at sixty-five, having held a chair in the same faculty, with one ten-year interruption, since 1964. Retirement changes almost nothing about the work and a great deal about the geography: no faculty meetings, no examination boards, and thirty years of invitations from universities on four continents that he is now free to accept. The papers of everything written up to this date go to the university library seventeen years later, as the first tranche of the Vorlass.
suggested_refs: The first tranche of the Habermas Vorlass, transferred to Goethe University Frankfurt in 2011
sources: aktuelles.uni-frankfurt.de, 'New insights into Jürgen Habermas' intellectual contributions'

segments.name: After the Chair: Prizes, Religion, and Europe

stops.name: Evanston, the permanent visiting professor
stops.date_confidence: attested that Habermas held a recurring 'permanent visiting professor' relationship with Northwestern University after the 1994 retirement (en.wikipedia). No start year, term pattern or department is given in any source consulted; 1995 is an ordering date immediately after the retirement and is not attested.
stops.campa: For years after the retirement he teaches a term at Northwestern, on the lake north of Chicago, where a generation of American political philosophers has grown up on translations of him. The arrangement is called a permanent visiting professorship. Nothing consulted gives the department, the starting year, or the pattern of the terms he taught. His English is careful and his speech still carries the operation of 1929, so the seminars go slowly and run on written handouts as much as on talk.
suggested_refs: Northwestern University, Evanston, and the American reception of discourse theory

stops.name: New York, the Theodor Heuss Professorship
stops.date_confidence: attested that Habermas held the Theodor Heuss Professorship at the New School (en.wikipedia; Wikipedia, 'The New School'). No year is given for the tenure in any source consulted and 1996 is an ordering date only. The chair is named for the first president of the Federal Republic and was endowed to bring German scholars to the school that took in the emigres of the 1930s.
stops.campa: The New School in Greenwich Village was the University in Exile, opened in 1933 to hold the scholars Germany was throwing out. Habermas holds its Theodor Heuss Professorship, a chair endowed to carry German thinkers to New York sixty years after the traffic had run the other way. The men whose institute he joined in 1956 had spent those same years in exile a few miles uptown, at Columbia. The lecture rooms are on Twelfth Street, several floors up, and hold about two hundred.
suggested_refs: The University in Exile, founded at the New School in 1933
The Institute for Social Research in exile at Columbia University, 429 West 117th Street

stops.name: Frankfurt, Paulskirche, faith and knowledge
stops.date_confidence: attested that Habermas received the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade in 2001, presented by Jan Philipp Reemtsma, and delivered the address 'Glauben und Wissen' (Wikipedia, 'Peace Prize of the German Book Trade'); the ceremony is customarily held in the Paulskirche during the Frankfurt Book Fair. The exact day, 14 October 2001, comes from the research pool's bibliography and was not re-verified against a printed programme.
stops.campa: A month after the towers come down he stands in the Paulskirche and speaks on faith and knowledge. Secular reason, he argues, cannot simply write religion off as a stage the species has walked through. It has to translate what religion has carried, the intuition of a wrong that cries out to heaven, into a language everyone can argue in, and it has to concede that it did not generate that content itself. Believers owe the translation too. Whether the address marks a change of position is argued at once and everywhere; he says it does not.
stops.quote: Egalitarian universalism, from which sprang the ideas of freedom and social solidarity, of an autonomous conduct of life and emancipation, of the individual morality of conscience, human rights, and democracy, is the direct heir to the judaic ethic of justice and the Christian ethic of love. This legacy, substantially unchanged, has been the object of continual critical appropriation and reinterpretation. To this day, there is no alternative to it.
suggested_refs: 'Glauben und Wissen', Peace Prize address, Paulskirche, Frankfurt, October 2001
sources: Wikipedia, 'Peace Prize of the German Book Trade'

stops.name: Paris, the joint article with Derrida
stops.date_confidence: the text is attested; both its date and Habermas's presence in Paris are open. Habermas and Jacques Derrida put their names to a joint piece treating the demonstrations of 15 February 2003 as the possible birth of a European public sphere and calling for a common European foreign policy. One strand of the research pool dated the stop to February 2003, which fuses the demonstrations with the essay about them; the correcting strand gives publication on 31 May 2003 in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung and simultaneously in Libération, and states plainly that it could not re-fetch that date because the session's search budget was exhausted. The 31 May date is used here and remains unverified. Habermas's physical presence in Paris is not established by anything consulted; the coordinate is the Paris pin already standard across the atlas's Frankfurt School files. That Derrida signed rather than co-drafted is widely reported and is not verified in this pool.
stops.campa: Fifteen million people march in the European capitals on one Saturday in February against a war their governments are joining, and two philosophers who spent the 1980s attacking each other in print decide the day means something. Habermas drafts the text; Jacques Derrida puts his name to it. It runs in a German paper and a French one at once and argues that Europe has just discovered it has a public, and should now be given a foreign policy to match. Nobody mentions the quarrel over iterability, which is twenty years old.
stops.quote: Global terrorism is extreme both in its lack of realistic goals and in its cynical exploitation of the vulnerability of complex systems.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy in a Time of Terror: Dialogues with Jürgen Habermas and Jacques Derrida, ed. Giovanna Borradori (University of Chicago Press, 2003), p. 34.
suggested_refs: 'Der 15. Februar oder: Was die Europäer verbindet', published jointly in the FAZ and Libération, 2003

stops.name: Munich, the dialogue with Cardinal Ratzinger
stops.date_confidence: attested as to event and venue, contradictory as to day. A structured dialogue with Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger on the prepolitical moral foundations of the democratic state, held at the Katholische Akademie in Bayern in Munich and published as Dialektik der Säkularisierung. en.wikipedia gives 14 January 2004; the Academy's own proceedings and German scholarship use 19 January 2004. The contradiction is recorded and not resolved; 14 January is used because it is the reading the pool tags attested. The coordinate lies within about 200 m of the Academy, which de.wikipedia places at 48.160/11.5914. The quote is from The Future of Human Nature and is the opening of a longer passage verified at en.wikiquote.org.
stops.campa: The Bavarian Catholic Academy puts a secular philosopher and the prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on one platform and asks whether a liberal state can produce the moral resources it runs on. Habermas says it cannot generate them by itself and must not silence the traditions that carry them. Ratzinger says much the same from the other side and adds that reason too stands in need of correction. Fifteen months later the cardinal is elected pope. The transcript of the afternoon is published as Dialektik der Säkularisierung.
stops.quote: As historical and social beings we find ourselves always already in a linguistically structured lifeworld.
stops.quote_source: The Future of Human Nature (Polity Press, 2003), p. 10.
suggested_refs: Dialektik der Säkularisierung: über Vernunft und Religion (2005), the published transcript of the Munich dialogue

stops.name: Kyoto, the biographical roots
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by kyotoprize.org's own laureate page: the 2004 Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy, category Thought and Ethics, with the commemorative lecture given on 11 November 2004 at the Kyoto International Conference Center. All three strands of the research pool carried different and wrong coordinates for that building, 35.0116/135.7681, 35.0316/135.7864 and 35.0459/135.7847, the worst of them some 5.5 km out; en.wikipedia places ICC Kyoto at 35 degrees 03'40"N, 135 degrees 46'59"E, which is 35.0611/135.7831, and that is used. The lecture title reads 'Biographical Roots'; one rendering of the prize page prints 'Biological', which is a transcription error and not a variant title.
stops.campa: In Kyoto, at seventy-five, he gives the most personal lecture of his life and calls it 'Public Space and Political Public Sphere: The Biographical Roots of Two Motifs in My Thought'. He goes back to the cleft palate, the operations, the years of speaking to schoolmates who could not follow him, and says that a person who cannot make himself understood learns early that he is not self-sufficient, that language is not anybody's property, and that everything depends on the other person's willingness to keep listening.
suggested_refs: 'Public Space and Political Public Sphere: The Biographical Roots of Two Motifs in My Thought', Kyoto Prize commemorative lecture, 11 November 2004
sources: kyotoprize.org, laureate page for Jürgen Habermas

stops.name: Bergen, the Holberg Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested that Habermas received the Holberg International Memorial Prize in 2005 (Holberg Prize laureate records, cross-checked in the research pool). No month, day or ceremony detail was carried, so the date is defaulted; the coordinate is Bergen, where the prize is administered and conferred.
stops.campa: Norway's Holberg Prize, founded two years earlier for the humanities and the social sciences and paid at a scale meant to answer the Nobel's silence about them, goes to Habermas in its third year. It carries the name of Ludvig Holberg, born in Bergen in 1684, who wrote his comedies and his essays for a reading public then in the process of inventing itself. Inside eighteen months Habermas has taken the Kyoto Prize in Japan and this one in Bergen, and the two citations say much the same thing in different registers. He is seventy-six.
suggested_refs: The Holberg International Memorial Prize, University of Bergen

stops.name: Frankfurt, Westend, the ninetieth birthday lecture
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to detail. The research pool records a ninetieth-birthday lecture, 'Noch einmal: Zum Verhältnis von Moralität und Sittlichkeit', delivered at Goethe University on 19 June 2019 and sourced to en.wikipedia; neither title nor day was independently re-fetched. The coordinate is the Westend campus at Theodor-W.-Adorno-Platz, to which the philosophy faculty moved in 2001, and not the Bockenheim campus of his own teaching years.
stops.campa: The day after his ninetieth birthday he lectures at his own university on the relation of morality to ethical life, the Kantian question set against the Hegelian one, which he has been turning over since Heidelberg. The room is on a campus he never taught on: the faculty left Bockenheim in 2001 for a square named after Adorno. He is still writing. The two volumes on faith and knowledge in Western philosophy, some seventeen hundred pages, come out the same year.
suggested_refs: Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie, 2 vols. (2019)
The Westend campus of Goethe University at Theodor-W.-Adorno-Platz

stops.name: Abu Dhabi, the award taken and given back
stops.date_confidence: attested that Habermas was named Cultural Personality of the Year by the Sheikh Zayed Book Award, accepted, and then reversed the acceptance on 2 or 3 May 2021, saying he had not adequately clarified the award's institutional connection to the Abu Dhabi government, and that the prize money was not received (Wikipedia, 'Sheikh Zayed Book Award'; Wikipedia, 'Jürgen Habermas'). The award article frames the episode as a declined award and does not confirm the category label by name for 2021, so the label follows the research pool. He did not travel; the coordinate is the city that awards the prize and there is no ceremony venue to name.
stops.campa: At ninety-one he accepts an Emirati prize, the Sheikh Zayed Book Award's Cultural Personality of the Year, and then German and international reporting sets out what the award is attached to: a government that jails people for what they publish. He withdraws within days and says in public that he had not properly clarified the award's connection to the political system in Abu Dhabi, and that accepting it was a mistake. The money is never paid. Nothing about the episode requires him to leave Starnberg, and he never goes to Abu Dhabi at all.
suggested_refs: The Sheikh Zayed Book Award, 2021, and Habermas's public withdrawal of 2-3 May 2021

stops.name: Göttingen, the death of his daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested: Rebekka Habermas, professor of modern history at Göttingen, died on 21 December 2023 at Göttingen after a long illness (de.wikipedia, 'Rebekka Habermas', which gives the day; de.wikipedia, 'Jürgen Habermas', which gives only December 2023). The coordinate is Göttingen, where she held her chair and died, and not her father's residence; his own presence there is not attested.
stops.campa: His second child, born in Frankfurt in 1959 while he was still an assistant on a contract Horkheimer wanted ended, dies at sixty-four in Göttingen, where she had held the chair in modern history for a quarter of a century and written on German colonialism and on the ordinary crimes of the nineteenth century. He is ninety-four when it happens, and his wife of sixty-eight years is still living. He outlives his daughter by two years and three months. Nothing reachable records what he said about her death, then or afterward.
suggested_refs: Rebekka Habermas (3 July 1959, Frankfurt am Main - 21 December 2023, Göttingen)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the papers go to the library
stops.date_confidence: attested, and the research pool's hedge on this entry is dropped: Goethe University's own announcement records two tranches of the Vorlass, the first in 2011 covering the work up to the 1994 retirement, the second in February 2025 covering the following thirty years, with about ninety file folders of letters, boxes of birthday correspondence, and files from his private computer including unpublished manuscripts, and it names Siegfried Unseld, Hans-Ulrich Wehler and Mario Draghi among the correspondents. Cataloguing runs in the library's Arcinsys system, cross-referenced with the Kalliope database, and posthumous access is governed by Hessian archive law. Day within February not recorded, defaulted.
stops.campa: In February the second and much larger consignment reaches the university library: about ninety folders of letters, boxes of birthday mail, and the contents of the private computer he has worked on since 1994, unpublished manuscripts included. The correspondents the announcement names run from Siegfried Unseld, who published him for forty years, to Hans-Ulrich Wehler and Mario Draghi. He has promised the library his working library as well. The catalogue entries are being made while he is still alive to be asked about them.
suggested_refs: The Habermas Vorlass at the Goethe University library, Arcinsys and Kalliope catalogues
sources: aktuelles.uni-frankfurt.de, 'New insights into Jürgen Habermas' intellectual contributions'

stops.name: Starnberg, the death at home
stops.date_confidence: attested: Suhrkamp's death notice records that Habermas died at his home in Starnberg on 14 March 2026, aged ninety-six, and gives no cause; Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the same day that Germany and Europe had lost one of the most significant thinkers of our time (PBS NewsHour). No street address is documented anywhere consulted and the coordinate is the town. The objection to the artificial-intelligence naming proposal is from the Max Planck Society's obituary, which gives it no date. Ute Habermas-Wesselhoeft's death is placed in June 2025 by one strand of the research pool and tagged a reconstruction there; it is not asserted here.
stops.campa: He dies at home in Starnberg, on the lake where the institute stood, ninety-six years old. Suhrkamp, which published him from the beginning, announces it on the family's word and gives no cause. Among his last public interventions, according to the Max Planck Society's obituary, was an objection to a proposal to name an artificial-intelligence conflict-resolution system after him: human understanding, he said, cannot be delegated to a machine. The Chancellor calls him one of the most significant thinkers of our time.
suggested_refs: Suhrkamp Verlag's death notice, 'Zum Tod von Jürgen Habermas'
mpg.de, 'Remembering Jürgen Habermas'
sources: pbs.org, 'Influential German philosopher Jürgen Habermas dies at 96'

stops.name: Söcking, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested: burial at the Söcking cemetery in Starnberg on 20 March 2026, with a graveside sermon by the Munich theologian Friedrich Wilhelm Graf, published in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on 1 April 2026 as 'Predigt am Sarge von Jürgen Habermas' (habermasforum.dk; the burial also recorded by de.wikipedia). The research pool carried three coordinates for the grave, 47.9998/11.3178, 47.9958/11.3311 and a Starnberg town-centre point; 48.0014/11.3153 is de.wikipedia's coordinate for Söcking bei Starnberg and is used. The pool also attributed to Graf a closing formula commending Habermas's life into God's hands; that phrasing was not found in the reachable summary and is not printed here.
stops.campa: He is buried in the village cemetery at Söcking, above the lake, six days after the death. A Protestant theologian he had argued with for years preaches at the coffin and repeats what Habermas once told him, that he was not really a believer, along with his own answer, that he was not a hardline atheist either. Then Graf says the thing the dead man's whole apparatus was built around: that death is the final cessation of all communication, and that they can no longer tell him what they would have liked to tell him.
stops.quote: You know that I am not really a believer.
stops.quote_source: Habermas to Friedrich Wilhelm Graf, recalled in Graf's graveside sermon at Söcking, 20 March 2026, published in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 1 April 2026.
suggested_refs: Friedrich Wilhelm Graf, 'Predigt am Sarge von Jürgen Habermas', Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 1 April 2026

stops.name: Frankfurt, Paulskirche, the memorial
stops.date_confidence: attested: a state memorial ceremony was held on Friday 19 June 2026 in Frankfurt's Paulskirche, with addresses by Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the historian Norbert Frei on 'Jürgen Habermas and the Federal Republic of Germany', and the philosopher Cristina Lafont on his philosophical legacy; a parallel academic symposium ran the same day at Goethe University's Westend campus, with a keynote by Axel Honneth, 'Der normative Eigensinn des Anderen: Habermas im Dialog mit Adorno', livestreamed in English (habermasforum.dk). Habermas was of course not present at either; the stop records events held for him in a building he had twice stood in as a laureate.
stops.campa: The republic holds his memorial in the church where its first parliament failed in 1848, the same room where he took the Adorno Prize in 1980 and the peace prize of the book trade in 2001. The head of state speaks; a historian speaks on what he had been to the Federal Republic; a philosopher speaks on what he leaves the discipline. Across the city that afternoon his own university runs a symposium, and Axel Honneth lectures on Habermas in dialogue with Adorno.
suggested_refs: The state memorial ceremony in the Paulskirche, 19 June 2026
The Goethe University memorial symposium of the same day, with Axel Honneth's keynote
sources: habermasforum.dk, 'Memorial ceremony for Habermas in Frankfurt's Paulskirche'
habermasforum.dk, 'Frankfurt symposium in memory of Jürgen Habermas'
